I am fairly confident that only blocking JavaScript will not help you with this type of tracking. Here's why:

If a company (think as large as Google) can instruct all popular websites which it owns or has influence over - to serve a single pixel (a logo, background graphics, whatever) to all visitors and you log in to just one of these websites and later browse to another website while still using the same IP, you can be uniquely identified since these websites are working together (by simply putting their logs together). In fact, not even serving special pixels/identifying elements is required, all they need to do is put their logs together (which is standard practice if you are a large corporation which provides multiple services like email, video hosting, social networking etc).

Some of the ways to try and improve your privacy while browsing the web is:

  • change your IP and browser agent every time you switch from a website and visit another website, never use the same IP twice
  • block javascript, flash, java and only allow pure HTML
  • block requests to download content from external domains if you browse only 1 domain
  • never log in anywhere where your email or personal info is required, or, use guerilla mail or similar services

Basically, TOR should help you achieve very good privacy (not perfect), but using TOR will most likely make you more interesting for government agencies.

In essence, the entire internet architecture as we know it needs to be revamped in such way that no device could be uniquely identified (dropping IP altogether, among other things).

The thing is, most hardware we use today is not open source, so you can very much count on that there are key-loggers/backdoors built into your motherboard, your router, your mobile phone, tablet any pretty much anything else which can connect to the internet.

Imagine this scenario if you use the same IP to browse for hours on end (many people keep the same IP for months because changing your IP is a hassle or expensive without using services like TOR):

  • you login to gmail, check your email, log out (using whatever device or browser)
  • you now clear your cookies, browser history, heck, even switch to a whole new computer or device
  • you visit youtube and watch a few clips
  • you visit google and do a few searches

Here is what google now knows about you:

  • even though you may not have an account on youtube, google now knows exactly which videos you watched, when and how long
  • google now knows what you searched for on google search engine and which websites you visited from their search results and when

All of this is now easily directly linked to you through your IP if you used the same IP for all steps above. How? Google can put together logs from their search engine, youtube and gmail and join them using your IP. So, google now knows who you are (if your gmail account uses real name and you communicate with people who don't care about privacy) and this data can and is easily acquired by government agencies as google is required by law to comply with government requests for information.

These are only 3 services I took as a simple example.

Now imagine how many popular services are owned by large corporations without anyone even knowing it (through sister companies) and how all this data about you can easily be put together, creating one large file about your internet usage habits, directly linked to your person. Scary, isn't it? :)
